cards.heading: What to check
cards.body: A client needs four things to reach other networks: an IP address, a subnet mask (prefix), a default gateway in the same subnet, and DNS servers. A 169.254.x.x address means DHCP failed.

cards.heading: Windows
cards.body: ipconfig shows the basics; ipconfig /all adds the MAC address, DHCP server, lease times and DNS servers. ipconfig /release and /renew request a new DHCP lease.
cards.example:
C:\> ipconfig /all
   Physical Address. . . : 00-50-56-C0-00-08
   DHCP Enabled. . . . . : Yes
   IPv4 Address. . . . . : 192.168.1.20(Preferred)
   Subnet Mask . . . . . : 255.255.255.0
   Default Gateway . . . : 192.168.1.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . : 192.168.1.1

cards.heading: macOS and Linux
cards.body: macOS: ifconfig (or networksetup -getinfo Wi-Fi). Linux: ip address (ip addr) for addresses, ip route for the default gateway, and /etc/resolv.conf (or resolvectl) for DNS. Older Linux tools: ifconfig and route -n.
cards.example:
$ ip addr show eth0
    inet 192.168.1.30/24 brd 192.168.1.255 scope global eth0
$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

cards.heading: Sanity checks
cards.body: Is the gateway inside the host's subnet? Is the mask the same as the router's? Is the host using the network or broadcast address? Each mistake stops traffic leaving the subnet. If the PC can ping an internet IP address such as 8.8.8.8 but not a name such as www.example.com, the address, mask and gateway are fine and the DNS server setting is the likely fault (test with nslookup). ipconfig /flushdns clears the DNS cache.
